title: The tyger
hookLine: hammer, chain, furnace, anvil: Blake asks a burning tiger, did he who made the lamb make thee? (The Tyger)
tomorrow: so who made the lamb? Blake lets a child answer.

lines: THE FORGE, THE HAMMER, THE HISS.
cards: Stand near a blacksmith's forge and it's all noise: the roar of the fire, the ring of the hammer, the hiss when hot iron hits the water. One poem by William Blake sounds like that. Blake was an engraver.
The stories of his life tell how he etched his poems into copper plates himself, printed them, and colored the pages by hand, with his wife Catherine helping.
On one plate, a tiger, and these lines: "Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night; / What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?"

teach.b: Then the poem becomes a workshop: "What the hammer? what the chain, / In what furnace was thy brain?" Hammer, chain, furnace, anvil. The poem asks and asks.
Near the end comes this: "Did he smile his work to see? / Did he who made the Lamb make thee?" Blake doesn't answer it. He asks it the way the Bible does.
Back to Job, and the whirlwind we met with Hopkins, but a different part of it.
In the Book of Job, when Job demands an explanation for his suffering, God answers with a tour of fierce creatures: the war horse, the wild ass, the leviathan no one can tame.

teach.h: JOB: DOTH THE HAWK FLY BY THY WISDOM?
teach.b: And this: "Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?" The Bible doesn't shrink the fierce things or blame them on someone else. It says God made them, and their wildness is beyond us.

teach.h: THE MAKER OF THE TERRIBLE TOO.
teach.b: That's the teaching under The Tyger: the maker of the gentle is the maker of the terrible too, and faith is left in awe, not holding an explanation. Blake added a teaching of his own.
In The Marriage of Heaven and Hell he wrote: "Without Contraries is no progression." The tiger and the lamb aren't a mistake in creation. They're contraries, and the world needs both.
Fittingly, Blake put The Tyger in his Songs of Experience, and its partner, The Lamb, in his Songs of Innocence.

how: Jewish and Christian readers turn to God's speeches from the whirlwind in Job 38-41 as a lesson in awe before creation; Blake's Songs of Innocence and of Experience are read and sung, and his hand-colored copies are kept in museums and libraries.

o: a fable of a wild beast tamed by a gentle child
Blake's poem of questions to a fierce, burning creature

s: The Tyger ends by answering who made the tiger
the poem is all questions, and the last one is left open.
Blake printed and colored his own books by hand
the stories of his life tell of Catherine helping him.
in Job, God avoids talking about fierce creatures
God points Job right at them: doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom?

games.q: on a nature show, a lioness takes down a gazelle. your kid asks, why would God make that? what fits Blake and Job?
o: it's a question believers ask too; the maker of the gentle made the fierce, and it's beyond us.
God didn't make lions; only the gentle animals come from God.
the gazelle must have done something wrong to deserve it.
games.why: Blake asks, did he who made the Lamb make thee? and Job's God points to the hawk and the leviathan. both leave the fierce in God's hands, and leave us in awe.

practice: Put your hand flat on your chest and find your heartbeat. Blake asks the tiger what dread hand was there when its heart began to beat.
For two minutes, feel your own heart hammering away, steady and fierce, and let that question sit without an answer.

wordCard.voice: The tyger: Blake's poem of questions to a fierce, burning creature, in Blake's own spelling. It asks who could make something so beautiful and so frightening, and leaves the answer open.

carryVoice: For the road: who made the tyger, and did he smile his work to see? See you at the lamb.
